_about: Copy for the two switching guides (compare-*.html; the URLs are kept from when they were comparison pages) and the trust page (trust.html), read by scripts/make-marketing-pages.mjs. RULES. (1) Every sentence about the studio claims only what the code does today; `ours` names the file that proves it, for whoever re-checks (it is not printed). (2) THE OTHER PRODUCT'S FACTS ARE NOT PRINTED until somebody has read them on the vendor's own page. Each one is a `rows` entry with the vendor's `source` URL, the `checked` day and a `status`: "unread" (taken from a search engine's summary of the vendor's page on 26 Oct 2026, when the vendor sites did not resolve from the sandbox this was written in; the `method` says so) or "read" (a person opened the source and confirmed the sentence on `checked`). The generator RENDERS ONLY "read" rows, with their source link and checked date beside them; test:marketing fails when an unread row's words reach a page. Today none is read, so the pages are switching guides that state our own facts only. OWNER STEP: open each source URL in a browser, correct or drop the row, then set `status` to "read" and `checked` to that day; the table appears on the next npm run make:marketing. (3) No superlatives, no 'better than', no disparagement, and nothing about what the other product can or cannot export: the steps say what the studio reads and let the reader check their own tool. (4) The names are other companies' trademarks, used only to describe their products; the page says so.

body: The Screenplay Writer's Import Screenplay reads these files. Each is read in your browser; nothing is uploaded to read it.
list: Final Draft (.fdx). Every line's type is already in the file, so nothing is guessed, and a locked scene number such as 12A comes across as it is.
Fountain (.fountain or .spmd), the plain-text screenplay format.
Word (.docx). Lines are placed by their screenplay style names (Scene Heading, Character and so on), or by their indents when the file has no such styles.
Plain text (.txt), laid out as a screenplay or written as Fountain.
A PDF with real text in it. A scanned or password-protected PDF is refused with the reason, rather than read wrongly.
Or paste the screenplay's text straight into the import window.

steps.name: Save a copy from your current tool
steps.text: Save or export your script in one of the formats above. Check your tool's own help for which of them it can write; a Final Draft (.fdx) file carries the most, because every line's type is in it.

steps.name: Open Import Screenplay
steps.text: In a project of your own, open the Screenplay Writer and choose File, then Import Screenplay. Choose the file, or paste the text.

steps.name: Read the preview
steps.text: Before anything is written, the import says how it read the file: as which format, and how many lines, pages and scenes it found.

steps.name: Choose where it goes
steps.text: If the screenplay already has pages, choose to add the import after them or to replace them. Replacing saves a draft of what was there first, and the old scene rows go to the scene bin rather than being deleted.

steps.name: Carry on from the scenes
steps.text: The script's scene headings become the project's scene list, which the breakdown, the stripboard and the call sheets read, on the plans that include those tools.

trust.sub: A script is months of work. Here is, in plain words, where it is kept, how you get it out, and who can read it.

sections.h2: It comes out in open formats
body: The screenplay exports as PDF, Word (.docx), Final Draft (.fdx) and Fountain from the Screenplay Writer's File menu. Fountain is plain text and Final Draft files open in most screenwriting programs, so a script written here can be carried on elsewhere.

The breakdown's element index, the shot list, script notes and the budget download as CSV for a spreadsheet, on the plans that include those tools. A backup file holds every project in your studio and restores into any browser from the same menu.
sections.check: Export a Fountain file on day one and open it in another app. That is the quickest way to see what travels.

sections.h2: It is saved in your browser first
body: Every change is written to your own browser's storage on your device before anything else happens. When you are signed in and sync is on, your projects also go to the studio's cloud so they reach your other devices. You can switch sync off in Settings; the copy in your browser stays either way.

That copy is read by the studio itself: it is not a file you can open in another program. Clearing your browser's site data removes it from that device, so keep a backup file or a Drive backup as well.

sections.h2: A backup in your own Google Drive
body: On Intermediate and Pro the studio can keep a backup file of your studio in your own Google Drive. It uses Google's drive.file permission, which lets it see only the files it created, never anything else in your Drive.
The file belongs to you: you can open, download or delete it from Drive at any time, and disconnecting Drive never deletes it.

sections.h2: It keeps working when the signal drops
body: The studio installs like an app and caches itself, so you can write, move strips and print call sheets on set without a connection. It keeps opening without a signal for up to 14 days after it last checked your sign-in online on that device; after that it needs a connection once to check your sign-in and plan. Until then your work is hidden, never deleted: it is still in your browser when the check succeeds.

A synced project can be reached only by you and the people you give access to. The database checks every request against the signed-in account, so a share link you make (to view, comment or edit) is what lets someone else in, and it ends when it expires or you remove it.

Our administrators can see account and payment records, but the console does not show your project content. As the operator of the database we can technically reach synced content; we do not open it unless you ask us to help, you ask for your data, or the law requires it. The privacy policy lists every case.

link.label: Read who can see your data

body: What you keep without us: every file you exported (PDF, Word, Final Draft, Fountain, CSV) and every backup file or Drive backup you made. Those are files on your own device or in your own Drive, and the screenplay formats open in other programs.

What depends on us: signing in, sync between devices, and opening the studio itself, which is also the only way to read the copy in your browser. Without our server the studio opens for at most 14 days after its last online check; after that the browser copy stays on the device but stays hidden. Our terms say that if we ever discontinue the service, we will give members reasonable notice and a way to export their synced data. So keep your own exports: they are the copy no company can take away.
